title: Introducing Instruction-Accurate Simulators for Performance Estimation of Autotuning Workloads
problem: Autotuning ML workloads typically requires execution on target hardware to evaluate implementation variants, but target hardware availability is limited. Scalability is constrained by hardware access when exploring large optimization spaces.
motivation: ML workloads have exponentially large optimization spaces; parallel simulation on accessible hardware would accelerate autotuning without waiting for target hardware.
method: The framework runs different versions of code on simulated computers—programs that mimic exactly how real processors execute instructions—instead of needing actual hardware. Machine learning models trained on statistics from these simulations predict how each code version would perform on real hardware. When tested on simulators for x86, ARM, and RISC-V processors (three common processor types), the models consistently ranked the fastest implementation in the top 3% of all tested versions.
key_novelty: Replacing actual hardware execution with simulated computers and machine learning predictions when searching for the fastest way to run ML code.
contributions: Simulation-based autotuning framework enabling parallel evaluation on accessible hardware
ML predictors achieving top-3% accuracy in identifying best implementations across x86/ARM/RISC-V
Outperforms native target execution for embedded architectures when running as few as 3 parallel simulations

metrics.other: best implementation within top 3% of predictions; outperforms native execution for embedded
